title: The Credential Won Twice: Erlangen, Göttingen, and the Cloister at Bryn Mawr
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Erlangen, Hauptstraße 23
stops.date_confidence: attested. MacTutor gives the birth date and the street address at Hauptstraße 23, Erlangen. Coordinate corrected against Nominatim to 49.5968, 11.0039; the research pool's 11.0118 lands about 570 m east, outside the Stadtmauer and off Hauptstraße entirely. Also corrected here: Max Noether came to Erlangen in 1875 as ausserordentlicher professor and was made ordinary professor only on 16 April 1888, so the campa does not call him a full professor at her birth.
stops.campa: Amalie Emmy Noether is born in the house at Hauptstraße 23, inside the old town wall, first child of Max Noether and Ida Amalia Kaufmann. The father teaches algebraic geometry at the university up the street, an assimilated Jew in a Bavarian town where that is a manageable thing to be. Three brothers follow her. The household runs on mathematics the way other households run on trade or on land: the subject is at the table, and it is what the visitors come to argue about. Bavaria does not admit women to its universities.
suggested_refs: Hauptstraße 23, Erlangen, the Noether family house at the time of her birth

stops.name: Erlangen, the school on Fahrstraße
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 1888-1889 by MacTutor, which names the Fahrstraße elementary school; no month or day is recorded, and September orders the stop at the start of a school year. Coordinate is approximate to the street, carried from the research pool, and not fixed to a surviving building.
stops.campa: She is sent to the elementary school on Fahrstraße, a few minutes on foot from the house, and nothing in the surviving record marks her out there. What comes down from these years is thin: enrollment, the ordinary progress of an ordinary Erlangen childhood, no prodigy story a biographer can lean on. What is already fixed, before she can do long division, is the corridor. Bavarian schooling for girls and Bavarian schooling for boys run alongside each other from this age, and only one of the two ends at a university gate.
suggested_refs: The Fahrstraße elementary school, Erlangen

stops.name: Erlangen, the Städtische Höhere Töchterschule
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1889 by MacTutor, which names the municipal higher school for daughters on Friedrichstraße and its curriculum of languages, arithmetic, music and domestic subjects. Month and day are not recorded; September orders the stop at the start of a school year. Coordinate approximate to the street.
stops.campa: From nine she attends the municipal higher school for daughters on Friedrichstraße: French, English, arithmetic, music, needlework, the running of a house. It is a decent school and it teaches her nothing that counts. The Gymnasium across town, where the boys read Greek and Latin toward the Abitur, is the only road to matriculation, and no girl walks it. She spends eight years here, then two more qualifying to teach exactly this curriculum to the next set of girls. The certificate at the end of them is dated 1900.
suggested_refs: The Städtische Höhere Töchterschule, Friedrichstraße, Erlangen

stops.name: Erlangen, the apartment on Nürnberger Straße
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1892 by MacTutor for the family's move to a larger apartment on Nürnberger Straße; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate corrected against Nominatim to about 49.5900, 11.0070; the research pool's 11.0145 sits some 550 m east of the street, which runs through the Innenstadt at about lng 11.007.
stops.campa: The family takes a larger apartment on Nürnberger Straße, and this address holds her through school, through the years of auditing, through the doctorate, and through the seven unpaid years after it. Max Noether's study is inside it and his students come to it. When his health gives way, his daughter walks from this door to the Mathematical Institute and delivers his lecture courses for him, with no appointment, no salary, and her name nowhere on the announcement. She is thirty-three before she lives anywhere else.
suggested_refs: Nürnberger Straße 32, Erlangen, the Noether family apartment from 1892

stops.name: Erlangen, the state examination in English and French
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900 by MacTutor, including the overall grade of very good and the weakest mark being for classroom delivery; month and day are not recorded and April only orders the stop before the autumn auditing. No source consulted names the building the examination was sat in, so the pin is the corpus canonical Erlangen coordinate inherited byte-identical from felix_klein.journey.json.
stops.campa: At eighteen she sits the Bavarian state examination and passes it, certified to teach English and French in schools for girls. The overall mark is very good. The one weak mark is for delivery in front of a class. She now holds a professional qualification, the only kind the kingdom is offering her, and a settled respectable career stands open in front of her. She never takes a teaching post. She goes instead to the university where her father lectures and asks the professors, one by one, for permission to sit at the back of the room.
suggested_refs: The Bavarian state teaching examination for English and French, 1900

stops.name: University of Erlangen, two women among a thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1900-1902 by MacTutor: auditing mathematics, Romance languages and history with each lecturer's individual permission, as one of two women among roughly a thousand students. Month defaulted to October for the start of the winter semester. Corpus canonical Erlangen pin, inherited byte-identical from felix_klein.journey.json.
stops.campa: Women cannot matriculate in Bavaria, but a lecturer may admit one to his room if he chooses. She asks, and is admitted, and audits mathematics, Romance languages and history for two years as one of two women in a student body of about a thousand. She holds no registration and no examination rights: she is a guest at every lecture, renewable by permission, in the faculty where her own father holds a chair. Two years of this, and then in 1903 she leaves for Nuremberg to sit the schoolboys' examination.
suggested_refs: Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen, the auditing years 1900-1902

stops.name: Nuremberg, the external Abitur
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14 July 1903 by MacTutor. Which of the Nuremberg Realgymnasien administered the examination is stated by no source consulted, and the coordinate is Nuremberg city centre, not a school building. This gap is stated in the campa rather than covered over.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of July she sits the matriculation examination at a Realgymnasium in Nuremberg, as an external candidate, having been taught none of it in any classroom. She passes. The paper is worth more than the teaching certificate she already holds: it is the credential that makes a university legally possible, the same sheet the boys of her year collect at eighteen and she collects at twenty-one. Which of the Nuremberg Realgymnasien it was, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: The external Abitur examination, Nuremberg, 14 July 1903

stops.name: Göttingen, one semester at the back of the room
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 1903-04 by MacTutor, which names Hilbert, Klein, Minkowski, Schwarzschild and Blumenthal as the lecturers she audited; month defaulted to October for the semester's start. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Göttingen pin 51.534, 9.935, inherited byte-identical from felix_klein.journey.json and heisenberg.journey.json; a rival Göttingen pin at 51.5413, 9.9158 exists in the oppenheimer and dirac files and is a standing corpus contradiction, not resolved here.
stops.campa: With the Abitur in hand she goes north to Göttingen for the winter and audits Hilbert, Felix Klein, Minkowski, Schwarzschild and Blumenthal, the strongest mathematics faculty in Europe assembled in one small Hanoverian town. She still cannot enroll anywhere. She listens for a single semester and goes home to Bavaria. Twelve years later two of the men in those rooms will write to her asking her to come back, because a problem has arrived on their desks that they cannot get to the bottom of and they think she can.
suggested_refs: The Göttingen mathematics lecture courses of winter semester 1903-04

stops.name: University of Erlangen, matriculation at last
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24 October 1904 by MacTutor, including that she now restricted herself to mathematics. Corpus canonical Erlangen pin, inherited byte-identical from felix_klein.journey.json.
stops.campa: Bavaria opens regular enrollment to women, and on the twenty-fourth of October she matriculates at Erlangen, twenty-two years old, in the university she has been attending as a guest for four years. She drops the languages and drops the history. From this date the record shows one subject only. The father's discipline becomes the daughter's. From this year both Noethers are publishing out of the same institute in the same small town, often on related problems, and the Erlangen mathematics faculty has two of them in it.
suggested_refs: Matriculation register of the Friedrich-Alexander-Universität, 24 October 1904

stops.name: Erlangen, the doctorate under Paul Gordan
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 December 1907 by MacTutor: the oral examination passed summa cum laude under Paul Gordan, on invariants of ternary biquadratic forms, the published thesis enumerating 331 covariants. The quote is verbatim from Auguste Dick's documentary biography, fetched as OCR from archive.org; only the single word is Noether's, and the framing sentence around it is Dick's, which is why the quote field carries one word and the source line says so.
stops.campa: Paul Gordan, the king of invariant theory, a computational algebraist who does everything by hand and by formula, takes her through a thesis on the invariants of ternary biquadratic forms. On the thirteenth of December she passes the oral summa cum laude. The published dissertation enumerates three hundred and thirty-one covariants, every one of them ground out by Gordan's methods. She will spend the rest of her working life dismantling exactly this way of doing mathematics, and she describes the thesis itself, afterwards, in a single word.
stops.quote_source: Emmy Noether on her own dissertation and the invariant-theory papers that followed it, reported in Auguste Dick, Emmy Noether 1882-1935; only the quoted word is verbatim Noether, the framing sentence is Dick's
suggested_refs: Noether, 'Über die Bildung des Formensystems der ternären biquadratischen Form' (Erlangen dissertation, 1907)
sources: Auguste Dick, Emmy Noether 1882-1935, archive.org OCR text

stops.name: Erlangen, the Mathematical Institute and no salary
stops.date_confidence: attested to roughly 1908-1915 by MacTutor: unpaid research at Erlangen's Mathematical Institute, substituting in her father's courses, with habilitation closed to women by German law and custom. No start month is recorded and 01-01 is the default. Corpus canonical Erlangen pin.
stops.campa: Doctorate in hand, she stays at the institute for seven years and is paid nothing for any of it. She publishes. She supervises. When Max Noether's health gives way she takes over his lecture courses and delivers them under his name. Habilitation, the qualification that would let her lecture as herself, is closed to women in Germany by law and by custom working together, so there is no next step to take and no salary to be reached by taking it. She is between twenty-six and thirty-three years old in this room.
suggested_refs: The Mathematical Institute of the University of Erlangen, 1908-1915

stops.name: Salzburg, the address to the Vereinigung
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1909 by MacTutor for both the address on invariant theory at the Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung meeting in Salzburg and her joining the society that year. Month and day are not recorded; September orders the stop at the society's usual autumn meeting season and is reconstruction.
stops.campa: She joins the Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung and speaks at its annual meeting in Salzburg on invariant theory. It is the first time she stands in front of the profession as herself and not as a substitute for her father. The society admits her without difficulty. The universities do not. Membership of the guild and employment by the guild are two separate questions in Germany, and she now has the first. She is twenty-seven, and the paper she reads is on the invariant theory she has spent five years inside.
suggested_refs: Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung annual meeting, Salzburg, 1909

stops.name: Erlangen, the decisive impulse from Ernst Fischer
stops.date_confidence: the quotation is verbatim from the MacTutor biography and is Noether's own statement about Fischer's influence, but MacTutor does not date the remark and this pass did not locate its original context. The date 1911 is reconstruction, chosen only to order the stop between Gordan's retirement and the Vienna lecture of 1913. Corpus canonical Erlangen pin.
stops.campa: Gordan retires, Ernst Fischer arrives in his place, and the direction of her work turns over. Where Gordan computed, Fischer argues from structure, from the arithmetic of the objects themselves rather than from formulas written about them. She later names this exchange, and not the doctorate, as the beginning of her actual mathematics. Everything she does at Göttingen over the next twenty years, every ring and ideal and chain condition, runs out of the turn she takes here. The institute where it happens does not employ her and cannot.
stops.quote: Above all I am indebted to Mr E Fischer from whom I received the decisive impulse to study abstract algebra from an arithmetical viewpoint, and this remained the governing idea for all my later work.
stops.quote_source: Emmy Noether, quoted verbatim in the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography, University of St Andrews
suggested_refs: Ernst Fischer's Erlangen years and the arithmetical turn in Noether's work

stops.name: Vienna, the Vereinigung and old Franz Mertens
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1913 by MacTutor: the lecture to the Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung in Vienna on fields of rational functions, and the visit to the aging Franz Mertens, whose grandson's later recollection concerned her appearance. Month and day are not recorded and September orders the stop; the coordinate is central Vienna, not a lecture hall.
stops.campa: She lectures to the mathematicians' society in Vienna on fields of rational functions, and while she is in the city she calls on Franz Mertens, who is old. A grandson of that household remembers her afterwards, and what he remembers is how she was dressed. This is the shape most contemporary recollection of her takes: the mathematics went into print under her own name, and the eyewitness testimony is about a woman's clothes and a woman's voice. She is thirty-one and has been publishing for six years.
suggested_refs: Franz Mertens in Vienna, visited during the 1913 Vereinigung meeting

stops.name: Göttingen, called north for Einstein's theory
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1915 by the University of Göttingen memorial page and by MacTutor: Hilbert and Klein bring her to Göttingen to work on invariant-theoretic questions arising from general relativity and from Hilbert's variational formulation of gravitation, with no position and no pay. Exact day not recorded, April is the recorded season. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Hilbert and Felix Klein send for her. General relativity has thrown up a problem in invariant theory that the Göttingen physicists cannot get to the bottom of, and they want the one person in Germany who has spent a decade inside the subject. She comes north with no position, no salary, and no right to lecture. The question waiting for her is this: in a theory where spacetime itself is one of the variables, what does conservation of energy even mean, and why does the quantity refuse to behave the way it does in every other physics?
suggested_refs: Hilbert's 1915 variational formulation of the gravitational field equations
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page

stops.name: Erlangen, the death of Ida Noether
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The fact that Ida Amalia Kaufmann Noether died suddenly shortly after Emmy's move to Göttingen is consistent with Dick's documentary biography as reported in the research dossier and with MacTutor's placement of the move in spring 1915, but no primary source confirming the exact month was fetched in this pass. May 1915 orders the stop and is not asserted as attested. Coordinate is the corrected Nürnberger Straße pin.
stops.campa: Weeks after the move north, her mother dies suddenly at the apartment on Nürnberger Straße. Emmy comes back to Erlangen to keep the house and look after her father, who is retired now and ailing, and works on the Göttingen problem out of her mother's rooms. The war is on and two of her brothers are in it. The household that raised her comes apart in the same season that the largest question of her working life is handed to her, and she carries both at once, in the same town, for months.
suggested_refs: Auguste Dick, Emmy Noether 1882-1935, on the family in 1915
sources: Auguste Dick, Emmy Noether 1882-1935, via the research dossier

stops.name: Göttingen, the habilitation refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 July 1915 by the University of Göttingen memorial page: the petition, Hilbert's and Klein's support, the Philosophical Faculty's rejection on grounds of her sex, and Hilbert's workaround of advertising courses under his own name. The two famous lines of this dispute are deliberately kept out of the prose as reconstruction: Hilbert's 'we are a university, not a bathhouse' survives only through later recollection, and Wikipedia notes his exact words were not preserved; the objection about soldiers learning at the feet of a woman is citable to Kimberling 1981 p. 14 and Lederman and Hill 2004 p. 72, from an unnamed faculty member, with no transcript. The research dossier's attribution of that second line to Dick is wrong, it does not occur in Dick's text. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: She petitions the Philosophical Faculty for the right to habilitate. Hilbert and Klein argue for her. The historians and philologists of the faculty argue that a Privatdozent is a member of the university and that a woman cannot be that, and the ministry agrees with them. The petition fails on the ground of her sex, stated plainly and in writing. Hilbert's answer is to advertise the courses under his own name and have her give them, so that the lectures happen on the timetable and the lecturer does not officially exist.
suggested_refs: Clark Kimberling, 'Emmy Noether and Her Influence', in Brewer and Smith (eds.), Emmy Noether: A Tribute to Her Life and Work (1981), p. 14, on the objections raised at the faculty meeting
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page

stops.name: Göttingen, Klein reads the paper to the Society
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia confirms that Klein presented Invariante Variationsprobleme to the Royal Society of Sciences at Göttingen on 26 July 1918; the arXiv English translation, physics/0503066, confirms the publication record in the Göttinger Nachrichten 1918, pp. 235-257. Coordinate corrected against Nominatim to the Akademie der Wissenschaften, Theaterstraße 7, at 51.5346, 9.9373; the research pool's 51.5322, 9.9354 is about 280 m off. This is the one stop in the file that departs from the canonical Göttingen pin, because the building is specifically identified.
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of July, in the Academy building on Theaterstraße, Felix Klein stands up and reads Invariante Variationsprobleme into the record of the Royal Society of Sciences. He does it because she is not permitted to. The paper proves two theorems. Every continuous symmetry of an action yields a conserved quantity; and a symmetry that depends on arbitrary functions, as general relativity's does, yields not a conservation law but identities among the field equations. What had looked like a defect in general relativity turns out to be a consequence of its own symmetry.
suggested_refs: Noether, 'Invariante Variationsprobleme', Nachrichten der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen (1918), pp. 235-257; M. A. Tavel's English translation, arXiv physics/0503066

stops.name: Göttingen, the habilitation accepted
stops.date_confidence: the year 1919 and the removal of the formal bar after the German Revolution are attested by the University of Göttingen memorial page. The precise date of 4 June 1919, and a May 1919 oral examination, are dossier-only and are reconstruction: neither was confirmed against a Göttingen record in this pass. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: The empire falls, the republic is declared, and the rule that a woman cannot be a Privatdozent goes with it. The faculty that refused her in 1915 accepts her habilitation in 1919. She may now lecture in her own name, examine, and be examined on her own work, and she is still paid nothing whatever, because the venia legendi carries the right to teach and no money attached to it. She is thirty-seven, and sixteen years have gone by since the Nuremberg Abitur.
suggested_refs: The Göttingen habilitation file of Emmy Noether, 1919
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page

stops.name: Göttingen, lecturing under her own name
stops.date_confidence: attested to winter semester 1919-20 by MacTutor for the start of lecturing in her own name, still unpaid; November orders the stop inside that semester and the day is not recorded. The characterisation of her teaching as thinking at the blackboard rather than delivering polished lectures is attested by MacTutor. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: Winter semester, and for the first time in her life the course announcement carries her own name. The lectures are not really lectures. She thinks at the blackboard, out loud, in front of whoever has come, going wrong and correcting herself and going on, so that the students are watching mathematics being made rather than reported. A good many of them cannot follow it at all. The ones who can never work any other way again. There is still no salary; she lives on what her family left her.
stops.quote: Like a too ripe fruit, it seemed to burst through the shell of your humanness. You were at once instrument of and receptacle for the intellectual force that surged forth from within you.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Weyl on Noether's creative power, funeral address, 18 April 1935, translated by Ian Beaumont; written sixteen years after this semester
suggested_refs: Göttingen course announcements, winter semester 1919-20

stops.name: Göttingen, Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1921 by MacTutor for the publication of Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen and for the ascending chain condition becoming central through it; month and day are not recorded and 01-01 is the default. The eponym Noetherian ring is attested through the standard literature and the bibliography in van der Waerden's 1935 obituary. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: The paper on ideal theory in rings appears, and with it the ascending chain condition moves to the centre of algebra. A ring in which every ascending chain of ideals stops is a ring where the whole classical decomposition theory can be recovered from one axiom about chains, with no computation and no case-by-case list. Rings that satisfy it are called Noetherian rings by everybody afterwards, in every algebra course on earth. The paper appears in Mathematische Annalen, volume 83, under her own name.
suggested_refs: Noether, 'Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen', Mathematische Annalen 83 (1921)

stops.name: Erlangen, the death of Max Noether
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 December 1921 by MacTutor for Max Noether's death at Erlangen, and to the same source for the postwar inflation eroding the family's resources. The coincidence of the calendar date with her own doctoral oral of 13 December 1907 is arithmetic on two attested dates, not a claim from any source. Coordinate is the corrected Nürnberger Straße pin.
stops.campa: Her father dies at Erlangen on the thirteenth of December, seventy-seven years old, having taught at the university in that town for forty-six of them. She had given his lectures for him when he could not stand up to give them. The inflation is beginning and what he leaves behind is not much, and it is the only money she will have for two more years. It is exactly fourteen years to the day since she stood in this same town and passed her doctoral oral.
suggested_refs: Max Noether's Erlangen chair, 1875-1919, and his death on 13 December 1921

stops.name: Göttingen, paid at forty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1923 by the University of Göttingen memorial page for the Lehrauftrag with a small fixed stipend, her first paid university position, at age 41; month unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. The 1922 title of nichtbeamteter ausserordentlicher Professor is attested by MacTutor. Correction applied: the research dossier's added clause that the 1923 stipend enabled her to supervise doctoral examinations is unsupported by anything checked and is dropped.
stops.campa: A Lehrauftrag for algebra is granted with a small fixed stipend attached, and Emmy Noether receives her first dependable income from a university at the age of forty-one, sixteen years after the doctorate. The year before, Prussia had given her the title of nichtbeamteter ausserordentlicher Professor, which conferred standing and no money; this confers money and no chair. She is not a civil servant, she accrues no pension rights, and she never will. What she has is a stipend, renewable, and a room to work in.
suggested_refs: The Göttingen Lehrauftrag für Algebra, 1923
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page

stops.name: Göttingen, Dedekind axiomatized
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1924 by MacTutor for the publication of Abstrakter Aufbau der Idealtheorie in algebraischen Zahlkörpern and for its axiomatization of Dedekind-type ideal theory; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin. Noted for the operator: Dedekind is a real one-directional relation for Noether, but there is no dedekind journey file in this checkout to interlock against.
stops.campa: Abstrakter Aufbau der Idealtheorie in algebraischen Zahlkörpern: the abstract construction of ideal theory in algebraic number fields. She takes Dedekind's nineteenth-century theory of ideals and states the handful of axioms a ring has to satisfy for the whole of it to follow. The particular number fields drop out of the argument. What is left is a short list of axioms, and any ring that satisfies them inherits the whole theory, in geometry or in topology as readily as in number theory.
suggested_refs: Noether, 'Abstrakter Aufbau der Idealtheorie in algebraischen Zahlkörpern', Mathematische Annalen 96 (1926)
Richard Dedekind's theory of ideals, the material she axiomatized

stops.name: Göttingen, the school in the seminar room
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 1923-1932 by MacTutor for the seminar style and for the students named: Grete Hermann, Max Deuring, Hans Fitting, Ernst Witt, Chiungtze Tsen, and for methods reaching print through them before her own name did. The year 1926 is a midpoint chosen to order the stop and is not a dated event. Van der Waerden's Moderne Algebra as the vehicle carrying her Göttingen lectures into general circulation is attested by MacTutor and Wikipedia. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: By the middle of the decade there is a Noether school. Grete Hermann, Max Deuring, Hans Fitting, Ernst Witt, Chiungtze Tsen and others work through her seminars and carry the methods out into their own papers, frequently into print before she has published the ideas herself. She does not appear to mind or to keep count. Van der Waerden sits in these rooms and turns what he hears into Moderne Algebra, the textbook that teaches the next two generations of algebraists and carries his name on the spine.
stops.quote: Not only did you give to your students intellectually - fully and without reserve - they gathered round you like chicks under the wings of a mother hen; you loved them, cared for them and lived with them in close community.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Weyl on the Noether school, funeral address, 18 April 1935, translated by Ian Beaumont
suggested_refs: B. L. van der Waerden, Moderne Algebra (Springer, 1930-31), built substantially on Noether's Göttingen lectures

stops.name: Bologna, the sectional address
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1928 by the University of Göttingen memorial page and MacTutor for the invited sectional address at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Bologna, on hypercomplex quantities and representation theory. The congress hall within Bologna is not confirmed by any source consulted; the coordinate is the corpus canonical Bologna pin, matching dante and other files.
stops.campa: The International Congress of Mathematicians meets at Bologna and she is invited to speak, on hypercomplex quantities and the theory of representations. Hypercomplex systems are what the next century will simply call algebras, and she is reorganizing the whole class of them from the top down. It is the first of two congress invitations that mark her as one of the leading algebraists alive. The invitation comes from the congress committee, she travels down from Göttingen to give it, and the address goes into the printed proceedings for 1928.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Bologna 1928
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page

stops.name: Moscow, the winter on Mokhovaya Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 1928-29 by MacTutor and Wikipedia for the visiting professorship at Moscow State University and for the work with Alexandrov, Pontryagin and Chebotaryov; correction applied to the research dossier, which dated it 1928 alone. November orders the stop inside the winter term. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 55.7558, 37.6176 is the Kremlin, and the Sparrow Hills main building did not exist until 1953. In 1928-29 the university occupied its old Mokhovaya Street campus, about 55.7560, 37.6122.
stops.campa: She spends the winter term as visiting professor at Moscow State University, in the old buildings on Mokhovaya Street across from the Kremlin, teaching abstract algebra and working with Pavel Alexandrov, Lev Pontryagin and Nikolai Chebotaryov. She likes the place and says so, in a decade when saying so is beginning to be written down. Five years later the file that removes her from Göttingen will cite her Marxist sympathies and her Russian contacts alongside her Jewish ancestry, and this winter is one of the entries in it.
suggested_refs: Moscow State University's Mokhovaya Street campus, its site until the 1953 move to the Sparrow Hills

stops.name: Frankfurt, a term away
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1930 by MacTutor for visiting teaching at Frankfurt; month and day are not recorded and 01-01 is the default. The named correspondents are attested individually elsewhere in the pool, Hasse through the 10 May 1933 letter, Artin through the shared 1932 prize and the 1934 Hamburg visit, Brauer through the 1934 Princeton audience, van der Waerden through Moderne Algebra, but the description of a single network is a characterisation and not a sourced claim.
stops.campa: A visiting term at Frankfurt. The German algebraists are a network now rather than a set of isolated chairs, and she is the node most of the lines run through. Hasse, Artin, Brauer, van der Waerden: correspondence, visits, joint theorems that end up carrying two or three surnames at once. Within three years the network will be scattered across three continents and the same letters will be carrying news about visas, dismissals, and who has managed to get a post. She is forty-eight.
suggested_refs: The Brauer-Hasse-Noether theorem (1932), one product of that correspondence

stops.name: Zürich, the plenary lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to the September 1932 International Congress of Mathematicians at Zürich by the University of Göttingen memorial page and MacTutor: the plenary lecture on hypercomplex systems in their relation to commutative algebra and number theory, the first ever given by a woman, with Karen Uhlenbeck the next 58 years later. The congress ran 5-12 September; the opening date is used to place the stop, and the specific day of her lecture is not recorded in anything consulted.
stops.campa: At the International Congress of Mathematicians in Zürich she gives a plenary lecture, on hypercomplex systems in their relations to commutative algebra and to number theory. No woman has ever done this. The next one to do it is Karen Uhlenbeck, fifty-eight years later. She is fifty years old, and the German university system has still not given her a chair. The lecture goes into the congress Verhandlungen, and she goes back to Göttingen to the same Lehrauftrag she left.
stops.quote: you were a great woman mathematician - I have no reservations in calling you the greatest that history has known.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Weyl, funeral address for Emmy Noether, 18 April 1935, translated by Ian Beaumont; spoken three years after the Zürich plenary
suggested_refs: Verhandlungen des Internationalen Mathematiker-Kongresses, Zürich 1932
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page

stops.name: Göttingen, the Ackermann-Teubner prize
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1932 by the University of Göttingen memorial page and MacTutor for the Alfred Ackermann-Teubner Memorial Prize shared with Emil Artin; no month is recorded and December orders the stop at the end of the year, before January 1933. Hermann Weyl's failed attempt in 1932 to have her elected to the Göttingen Academy of Sciences is carried from the interlock lens and the dossier and is reconstruction. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: The Alfred Ackermann-Teubner Memorial Prize for the Advancement of Mathematical Knowledge is awarded jointly to Emmy Noether and Emil Artin. It is the only prize of any consequence she receives in her lifetime, and she shares it. In the same year Hermann Weyl tries to have her elected to the Göttingen Academy of Sciences and does not succeed. She is fifty years old and has held the Lehrauftrag for nine years. Four months after the prize, the government changes.
suggested_refs: The Alfred Ackermann-Teubner Memorial Prize, 1932, shared with Emil Artin

segments.name: The Law of the Seventh of April

stops.name: Göttingen, the notice under paragraph three
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1933 by Wikipedia, which quotes the Prussian Ministry letter citing the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of 7 April 1933; the Göttingen memorial page confirms she was among the first faculty forced out but gives no date. The exact day of the letter is not recorded in anything consulted, and 25 April orders the stop between the law's promulgation and the 10 May letter to Hasse. This April notice is a Beurlaubung and is deliberately kept separate from the final withdrawal of the Lehrbefugnis in September; the research pool conflated the two. Quote verbatim from Dick's documentary biography, fetched as OCR. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service is promulgated on the seventh of April, and within weeks the Prussian ministry sends the letter that puts her out of the university on the ground of her ancestry. She is among the first at Göttingen to go. Writing to Helmut Hasse on the tenth of May she is more exercised about other people's positions than her own: she has a small inheritance, and she never had a pension to lose in the first place.
stops.quote: Many thanks for your dear, compassionate letter! I must say, though, that this thing is much less terrible for me than it is for many others. At least I have a small inheritance (I never was entitled to a pension, anyway) which allows me to sit back for a while and see.
stops.quote_source: Emmy Noether, letter to Helmut Hasse, 10 May 1933, in Auguste Dick, Emmy Noether 1882-1935
suggested_refs: The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, 7 April 1933, paragraph 3
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page
Auguste Dick, Emmy Noether 1882-1935, archive.org OCR text

stops.name: Göttingen, the seminar in her own apartment
stops.date_confidence: the seminar continuing in her own apartment after she was barred from the institute is attested only through Hermann Weyl's funeral address of 18 April 1935, a memorial recollection given two years after the events, not a contemporaneous record. No source consulted gives the apartment's address, so the stop sits at the corpus canonical Göttingen pin rather than at an invented street. June 1933 orders the stop between the April notice and the September withdrawal and is not a dated event. Quote verbatim from the St Andrews reproduction of Beaumont's translation.
stops.campa: Barred from the institute, she moves the seminar into her flat. Students come. One of them comes in the brown shirt of the SA, and she lets him in and teaches him, because it does not occur to her that a person who wants to learn algebra could be the same person who wants her gone. Weyl, describing this two years later at her graveside, does not offer it exactly as innocence. He offers it as a fact about her that had no exceptions anywhere in it.
stops.quote: Even those in their brown shirts were welcome; never for a second did you doubt their integrity.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Weyl, funeral address for Emmy Noether, 18 April 1935, translated by Ian Beaumont
suggested_refs: Hermann Weyl's funeral address, the only source for the apartment seminars of summer 1933
sources: Hermann Weyl, funeral address, 18 April 1935, reproduced at MacTutor History of Mathematics

stops.name: Göttingen, the Lehrbefugnis withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 September 1933 by de.wikipedia: 'wurde Noether am 13. September 1933 die Lehrbefugnis endgültig entzogen'. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: the research pool's geography lens gave 2 September 1933 and cited the Göttingen memorial page for it, but that page carries no date at all, saying only that in 1933 she was among the first to lose her position. The eleven-day discrepancy appears to be a dossier artifact. The additional grounds cited against her, her pacifism, her politics and her Soviet contacts, come from the Göttingen memorial page. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of September the permission to teach is withdrawn for good. The April letter had suspended her; this ends it. The file against her runs to more than her ancestry: her pacifism, her politics, the winter in Moscow, the Russian correspondents, all of it entered alongside the racial clause. Göttingen, which was the mathematical capital of the world on the day she arrived in 1915, empties within a single year, and she is one of the first out of the door. She had been on that faculty eighteen years, ten of them paid.
stops.quote: Her unselfish, significant work over a period of many years was rewarded by the new rulers of Germany with a dismissal, which cost her the means of maintaining her simple life and the opportunity to carry on her mathematical studies.
stops.quote_source: Albert Einstein, letter to the editor, New York Times, 4 May 1935
suggested_refs: The Göttingen personnel file recording the withdrawal of Noether's venia legendi, 13 September 1933
sources: University of Göttingen, 'Emmy Noether (1882 to 1935)' memorial page

stops.name: Bremerhaven, the Columbuskaje
stops.date_confidence: the crossing aboard the SS Bremen in October 1933 is attested by MacTutor; the departure port is inferred, not attested. Bremerhaven was North German Lloyd's terminal and the Bremen's standard port, but no fetched source names it for this sailing. Coordinate corrected to the Columbuskaje at 53.5607, 8.5529 per Nominatim; the research pool's 53.5396, 8.573 sits about 2.5 km inland, south of the Überseehafen. The Bryn Mawr offer behind the sailing, a one-year research professorship at 4,000 dollars arranged with the Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced German Scholars and dated 4 August 1933, is dossier-only and unverified here.
stops.campa: She boards the SS Bremen at the North German Lloyd quay and sails for New York. There is nothing clandestine about any of it: a dismissed professor with a passport, a berth, and a written offer from an American women's college, leaving the country legally at the invitation of a rescue committee. What she is carrying out is not in the luggage. It is a way of doing algebra that Germany has just decided it does not want, and that will be standard everywhere on earth within twenty years.
suggested_refs: The Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced German Scholars, which arranged the Bryn Mawr appointment

stops.name: New York, the harbour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The arrival date of 7 November 1933 is dossier-only and was not independently refetched in this pass; MacTutor gives only the October sailing and arrival in New York before Bryn Mawr. No pier is documented and the coordinate is a generic Manhattan harbour point. Einstein's arrival at Princeton on 17 October 1933 aboard the SS Westmoreland is attested in einstein.journey.json; the two crossings falling three weeks apart is arithmetic on those two dates.
stops.campa: She lands in New York in the first week of November, fifty-one years old, with a one-year contract in her pocket and no German position to go back to. Albert Einstein came off a ship into this same harbour three weeks earlier and went on to Princeton; she goes on to Bryn Mawr, fifty miles from him. Neither of them will see Germany again after the following summer. Which pier she docked at, who met her, and what she said on landing are recorded nowhere this pass could reach.
suggested_refs: Passenger manifests of the SS Bremen, autumn 1933

stops.name: Bryn Mawr College, three students and a textbook
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter term of 1933-34 by MacTutor and Wikipedia: a first seminar of three students and one staff participant, working through van der Waerden's Moderne Algebra. December orders the stop inside that term. Coordinate corrected against Nominatim to Bryn Mawr College at 40.0287, -75.3155; the research pool reused 40.0227, -75.3141 across five stops, which falls roughly 700 m south of campus, below Lancaster Avenue.
stops.campa: The first seminar at Bryn Mawr has three students and one member of staff in it, and they work through van der Waerden's Moderne Algebra. She is teaching, out of a book written by a student of hers, material she first taught in the room where he learned it. Her English is poor at the start and improves slowly; she talks fast and drops into German whenever the mathematics gets ahead of the vocabulary. The women in this room are the last cohort she trains.
suggested_refs: Bryn Mawr College graduate mathematics seminar, winter term 1933-34

stops.name: Princeton, old Fine Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1934 by MacTutor and Wikipedia for the start of weekly lectures at the Institute for Advanced Study on Flexner's and Veblen's invitation, with Albert, Vandiver, Brauer and Weyl attending. The IAS had no building of its own until 1939 and used Princeton University's old Fine Hall, so the pin is inherited byte-identical from dirac.journey.json rather than pointing at a later building. The remark about a men's university is reconstruction: the IAS institutional history page returned HTTP 403 on attempted fetch and it could not be confirmed, which is why it is reported as attributed and not used as a quote field.
stops.campa: From February she takes the train up to Princeton once a week to lecture at the Institute for Advanced Study, which is two years old, has no building of its own, and borrows rooms in Fine Hall. Flexner and Veblen invited her. Albert, Vandiver, Brauer and Weyl come to hear her. The arrangement is informal and she is not paid for it the way the visiting men are, and according to her circle there she remarked that Princeton was a men's university where nothing female was admitted.
suggested_refs: Old Fine Hall, Princeton, first home of the Institute for Advanced Study

stops.name: Hamburg, the word on the underground
stops.date_confidence: the summer 1934 return trip to Germany, including seeing her brother Fritz, visiting Göttingen and meeting Emil Artin in Hamburg, is attested by MacTutor; no month within the summer is recorded and July orders the stop. Natascha Artin's underground anecdote is reconstruction, a recollection recorded decades later. The Fritz Noether material is corrected from the research pool, which mis-tagged it and placed his death at Tomsk: he took the Tomsk chair in 1934, was arrested by the NKVD there in November 1937, sentenced to 25 years on 23 October 1938, sentenced to death on 8 September 1941 and shot at Oryol on 11 September 1941 in the Medvedev Forest massacre, rehabilitated 22 December 1988. Coordinate is central Hamburg, not a specific building.
stops.campa: On her last summer in Europe she goes to Hamburg to see Emil Artin, with whom she had shared the prize two years earlier. Natascha Artin remembered, decades afterwards, riding the underground beside her while she talked mathematics at full volume: Ideale, Gruppen, Führer, three ordinary technical words in German algebra, and the other passengers going rigid at the third of them. Her brother Fritz is leaving Germany too, for a chair at Tomsk in the Soviet Union. That decision has him shot at Oryol in 1941.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Fritz Noether', for the Tomsk chair, the 1937 arrest, and the Medvedev Forest executions of September 1941

stops.name: Göttingen, the last visit
stops.date_confidence: attested to summer 1934 by MacTutor for a final visit to Göttingen during the German return trip; no month or day is recorded and August orders the stop after the Hamburg meeting. Corpus canonical Göttingen pin. The absence of any written account by her of the visit is a stated gap, not an inference: nothing was located in this pass.
stops.campa: She goes back to Göttingen once, in the summer of her last European trip, and walks through a university that made her career and then took it off her inside a single year. The institute buildings are where they were. Most of the people in them are gone, dismissed or emigrated or dead. She does not stay long. She left nothing in writing about the visit that this pass could find; what is recorded is only that she went, and that she was back at Bryn Mawr in time for the autumn term.
suggested_refs: The Göttingen Mathematical Institute in 1934, after the emigration

stops.name: Bryn Mawr College, the second year
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1934-35 by MacTutor for the renewal of the Bryn Mawr appointment for a second year alongside the continuing Princeton lectures, with no permanent American chair secured; month unrecorded, October orders the stop at the start of the academic year. Weyl's judgement about her happiest years is his own, from the 1935 memorial material, and is a third-party characterisation rather than her statement. Corrected Bryn Mawr College coordinate.
stops.campa: The appointment is renewed for a second year. She keeps the seminar and keeps the weekly train to Princeton, and for the first time since 1908 she is employed, teaching under her own name, with graduate students who came specifically to work with her and nobody else. There is no permanent chair anywhere in America, and the renewal she is living on is again for one year only. Einstein will write afterwards that these were the happiest years of her career.
stops.quote: Farsighted friends of science in this country were fortunately able to make such arrangements at Bryn Mawr College and at Princeton that she found in America up to the day of her death not only colleagues who esteemed her friendship but grateful pupils whose enthusiasm made her last years the happiest and perhaps the most fruitful of her entire career.
stops.quote_source: Albert Einstein, letter to the editor, New York Times, 4 May 1935
suggested_refs: Bryn Mawr College appointment records, 1934-35

stops.name: Bryn Mawr Hospital, the fourth day
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14 April 1935 by MacTutor and Wikipedia: surgery for a pelvic mass, three days of apparently normal recovery, then circulatory collapse, unconsciousness and a temperature of 109 F (42.8 C), with cause given cautiously as probable postoperative infection. Coordinate corrected against Nominatim to Bryn Mawr Hospital, 130 S Bryn Mawr Avenue, at 40.0193, -75.3211; the research pool's 40.0186, -75.3129 is about 690 m off, and the afterlife lens gave a third, different coordinate for the same death.
stops.campa: A pelvic tumour is found and she is operated on. For three days she recovers normally and the surgery is called a success. On the fourth day her circulation collapses, she loses consciousness, and her temperature climbs to a hundred and nine degrees Fahrenheit. She dies the same afternoon, fifty-three years old. The cause is entered cautiously as a postoperative infection nobody can name, and the record does not resolve it any further than that; no autopsy report appears in anything reachable.
suggested_refs: Bryn Mawr Hospital, 130 South Bryn Mawr Avenue, site of the April 1935 surgery

stops.name: Bryn Mawr, the service at President Park's house
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 April 1935 by the St Andrews reproduction of Weyl's funeral address, which is dated and translated by Ian Beaumont following Peter Roquette. The venue, the home of Bryn Mawr president Marion Edwards Park, and Brauer's presence come from the same body of memorial material. Note that Weyl's long published memorial address is a separate text from these graveside remarks; the distinction is real and is preserved. Corrected Bryn Mawr College coordinate; the president's house is on campus and is not separately pinned.
stops.campa: A small service is held at the house of Marion Edwards Park, the college president who had arranged the rescue offer two years before. Hermann Weyl and Richard Brauer come down from Princeton. Weyl speaks in German, addressing a dead woman directly in the second person for the length of the address, and calls her the greatest woman mathematician history has known. Then he says the thing he actually came to say, which is not about mathematics at all but about the ground.
stops.quote: Your final rest will be in foreign soil, in the soil of this great hospitable country that offered you a place to carry on your work after your own country closed its doors on you.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Weyl, funeral address for Emmy Noether, Bryn Mawr, 18 April 1935, translated by Ian Beaumont
suggested_refs: Hermann Weyl, funeral address for Emmy Noether, 18 April 1935, and his separate published memorial address
sources: Hermann Weyl, funeral address, reproduced at MacTutor History of Mathematics

stops.name: Bryn Mawr College, the cloister of the Old Library
stops.date_confidence: the cremation and interment of the ashes under the walkway around the cloisters of the Old Library, formerly the M. Carey Thomas Library, are attested by both en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia. No source consulted gives the date of interment, and 20 April orders it after the 18 April service. Coordinate corrected to about 40.0280, -75.3148: the research pool offered two mutually inconsistent pins for this one spot, 40.0233, -75.3138 and 40.0234, -75.3116, both roughly 700 m to 1 km southeast of campus. Einstein's letter is dated by St Andrews: written at Princeton 1 May 1935, published in the New York Times 4 May 1935. Correction applied to the dossier's note, which claimed the page renders an umlaut-less Fraulein; the raw HTML reads Fräulein.
stops.campa: She is cremated, and the urn is set under the walkway that runs around the cloister of the Old Library, the building then called the M. Carey Thomas Library. There is no cemetery and no headstone in a field: the ashes lie under the paving of a walkway that students cross on their way to class, with nothing above ground marking the spot. Einstein writes to the New York Times from Princeton on the first of May, three weeks after the funeral, to put on the record what the profession had thought of her.
stops.quote: In the judgment of the most competent living mathematicians, Fräulein Noether was the most significant creative mathematical genius thus far produced since the higher education of women began.
stops.quote_source: Albert Einstein, letter to the editor, New York Times, 4 May 1935, written at Princeton on 1 May 1935
suggested_refs: The cloister of the M. Carey Thomas Library, Bryn Mawr College, where the ashes were interred
Einstein's letter to the New York Times, 4 May 1935, reproduced at MacTutor History of Mathematics

stops.name: Bryn Mawr, Goodhart Hall
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and not resolved. A larger memorial gathering in Goodhart Hall on 26 April 1935 comes from the research dossier's chronology, cross-checked only against MacTutor's general timeline; neither the date nor the venue could be confirmed against a Bryn Mawr record in this pass, and what is independently confirmable is only that Weyl's graveside speech was on 18 April. Coordinate corrected to about 40.0290, -75.3163; the pool's 40.0224, -75.3122 is roughly 900 m off campus. The posthumous names in the campa are separately attested: the eponyms through van der Waerden's 1935 bibliography and the standard literature, the lunar crater through the USGS and IAU Gazetteer Feature ID 4380 at 66.38 N, -114.19, 64.80 km across, approved 1970 and officially spelled Nöther, and the DFG Emmy Noether Programme through dfg.de, whose own page states no founding year, so the dossier's 1997 is not asserted.
stops.campa: A larger memorial is held in the college's assembly hall, beyond the handful who stood in the president's parlour. What comes afterwards is a vocabulary. Noetherian rings and modules, Noether normalization, the Lasker-Noether theorem, the Brauer-Hasse-Noether theorem, Noether currents, and the two theorems that go by her name alone. The German research foundation names its programme for young scientists after her. On the far side of the moon there is a crater called Nöther, sixty-five kilometres across.
stops.quote: Though decay take your mortal remains, we will always cherish the legacy you left us.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Weyl, closing line of the funeral address for Emmy Noether, 18 April 1935, translated by Ian Beaumont
